steps.text: Part 3 of 4: King and rook against king: fence, approach, check on the edge. This part covers When it fails; Mixed test. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.title: A check next to the king
steps.prompt: White can also check at once with Rg8+. Predict first: does that work as well as the best move? Then find the best move.

steps.text: **Why it works.** [I] Mate needs an edge: a king in the middle has eight squares, on an edge five, in a corner three. The check pushes the king back only when the kings face each other with one square between **and it is White's move**. Three things break the win: a rook within the king's reach, a quiet move that leaves Black no legal move, a check when the kings do not face.

steps.title: The rook is attacked
steps.prompt: The black king attacks the unguarded rook and it is White's move. Predict first: does the king move Kb2 keep the win as well as the best move? Then find a move that keeps the win.

steps.caption: The kings do not face each other: the white king stands a step to the side. A check now lets the black king step forward.

line.say: The rook checks along the seventh rank from far away.
The king steps forward to f6, which the white king does not guard. The squeeze has failed, and White must begin again.

claims.statement: After Ra7+ the black king has four squares, one of them in front.
White still wins from here, but not by that check.

steps.caption: The kings face each other with a gap, but it is White's move, so a check would not help. A waiting rook move passes the turn.

line.say: A waiting move [I]: the rook stays far away, nothing is attacked, and Black must now give up the facing position.

steps.text: **The waiting rule [I].** Check only when the kings face each other with one square between and it is White's move. Otherwise make a safe waiting move with the rook, far from the king, and let Black come to you. The boards above are checked with the tablebase; the rule is a teaching summary, not a theorem for every position.

steps.title: Mate or stalemate?
steps.prompt: Both Rg7 and the best move take the king's last square. Predict first: is Rg7 as good as the best move? Then find checkmate in one.

steps.caption: A rook beside the king, with nothing guarding it, is simply lost. It is Black's move.

line.say: The black king takes the unguarded rook. Two bare kings are left, and the game is a draw.

claims.statement: The rook on d2 is attacked and undefended.
The position is a draw with Black to move.

steps.text: **Stalemate, the quiet disaster.** If every square is taken away but the king is not in check, the game is drawn. It happens near the end, when the king is boxed in and White plays a quiet rook move. Before any move that is not a check, count Black's legal moves. If the count is zero, find another move.

steps.caption: Two rook moves take away the king's last squares. Only one of them is mate.

line.say: The rook checks along the a-file while the king on c8 covers b8 and b7. Checkmate.

claims.statement: Before the move the black king has only a7.
The other rook move, Rg7, is only a draw.

steps.caption: The other move, Rg7: the rook takes a7 and b7, the king on c8 takes b8, and Black has no move and is not in check.

steps.text: **Three questions before every move.** One: is my rook out of the king's reach, or guarded? Two: after my move, does Black still have a legal move, or is it mate? Three: does this move take away a square or a line that Black had? [I] These questions catch the two errors this lesson showed, a lost rook and a stalemate; they do not choose the best move.
